description: The single source of truth for every numeric budget the console is gated on. Rows carry a `scope`. A `product` row is one of the console's own product figures: every one of them appears here exactly once, whether or not this revision can measure it, because a budget silently omitted is a budget nobody notices is ungated. A `harness` row is a bound with no product figure behind it — whether the scaffolding applies it to itself or this harness applies it to a shipped artifact the product list does not bound in that unit — so its `specTarget` states the bound in its own terms while `harnessBudgetDerivation` states, once for the whole set, why those figures and not others. Both kinds live here for the same reason: one value, one home. An entry whose `status` is "n/a" is not measurable at this revision and names, in `notMeasurableReason`, what is missing. Every harness that reads this file prints one line per "n/a" entry beside the budgets it did measure.
harnessBudgetDerivation: A `harness` row is one with no product figure behind it, so where its number came from is this field's to say — stated once for the whole set, because a derivation copied into each row has as many places to drift as there are rows. There are two groups. THE FIVE `console-*` ROWS are the slices of ONE tier timeout, so their derivation is a property of that set and is stated here rather than five times over. Three of them bound the launch: `launch-deadline.ts` mints a single deadline per launch and divides it into readiness, the frame witness, and cleanup, so a launch that overruns produces its own diagnostic instead of vitest's undiagnosable kill. The other two bound what runs BETWEEN a settled launch and its cleanup — the caller's test body, which was budgeted by nothing until 2026-09-05 and could therefore be killed by vitest mid-poll, before the poll's own message or the cleanup settled, leaving an Electron alive. A launching tier's `testTimeout` is now DERIVED from these rows rather than written as a literal: `tierTimeoutFor()` in `launch-deadline.ts` sums the launch budget, the body allowance that tier applies, and a 2 000 ms settlement residual — a floor rather than a ceiling, which is why it is a constant beside those rows and not a row among them, since every row here is a ceiling. The `console-launch-cleanup` row is reserved TWICE inside that launch budget, because one cleanup spends it in two phases — the close it races, and then the termination loop that restarts the same figure when the close had to be abandoned — so a slice holding it once left the loop's whole deadline outside what the tier waits for (`CLEANUP_PHASES` in `launch-deadline.ts`, measured against the class's own end-to-end spend by `test/helpers/cleanup-slice-derivation.test.ts`). `test/helpers/launch-deadline.test.ts` resolves every launching tier through `createVitest` and holds its real `testTimeout` and `hookTimeout` against those derived figures, never against a literal copied out of the config. The body allowance is per tier because the two tiers' bodies are different subjects — a driven interaction against a sustained workload — and a tier that states none gets the shorter one, so a new tier fails loudly inside its own bound rather than quietly under vitest's. The figures are generous on purpose: a cold CI runner with no warm Electron cache is the case these must not flake on, and each is a ceiling for a wedged phase rather than an expectation. THE `renderer-initial-fonts` ROW bounds a shipped artifact rather than the scaffolding, and it sits in this scope for the reason the scope exists: the product list names eight rows and no font row, so a ninth `product` id would break the one claim that list's set is checkable by — that it names these and nothing else — while the bytes still need a ceiling. Its figure is derived from the faces themselves rather than picked. `src/renderer/src/console/frame/bindings/typeface.ts` declares ONE VARIABLE FILE PER FAMILY AND STYLE — the Roman and Italic Latin-1 splits of `@ibm/plex-sans-variable` and `@ibm/plex-mono-variable`, which the console's typography rules require — measuring 68 988 B and 80 188 B for the sans and 32 576 B and 38 688 B for the mono, 220 440 B in total on 2026-09-09. 232 000 B leaves 11 560 B — about 5.2 % — for a re-subset or a foundry version bump while still refusing a FIFTH font file on the initial graph: the smallest split either package publishes at these pins is 13 300 B (`IBM Plex Mono Var-Roman-Latin3.woff2`) — the row's own `refusalControlBytes`, which is where that figure lives so the harness that plants a control at exactly it reads the number rather than restating it — so any fifth file takes the total to at least 233 740 B, which is over. Refusing that file is the property the figure is chosen for, which is why it is not rounded up to the next convenient number — and it is why the headroom is 5.2 % rather than the ~10 % the smaller subject carried: ten percent of 220 440 B is 22 044 B, which is larger than the smallest file either package publishes, so a ten-percent ceiling would admit a fifth face and the refusal would stop holding. The two properties cannot both be had at this size, and the refusal is the one this row is worth having. THE CEILING MOVES WITH ITS SUBJECT, IN EITHER DIRECTION, AND ONLY WITH IT. It was tightened 130 000 → 112 000 in the edit that took the faces variable, because the six static cuts it replaced weighed 118 488 B and holding 130 000 over the 101 564 B that followed would have grown the slack from 9.7 % to 28 % — 130 000 admits a third file anywhere below 28 436 B, which is most of what these two packages publish. It was raised 112 000 → 232 000 on 2026-09-09 when the drawn italics landed, and that is the same rule rather than an exception to it: the console sets italic runs in both families, and a family declaring only its upright face renders those runs as a browser-synthesized oblique — a shear of the upright outlines, which the console's typography rules do not admit. That module's own header states which rules ask for it and counts them; the count is not restated here, because a figure with two homes is a figure that will disagree with itself. What grew is what the design ships, so the ceiling was re-derived over the four files it now ships; a ceiling is never widened to admit a reading that failed.

unitConventions.kB: 1000 bytes (SI). The spec writes `kB`; the SI reading is also the stricter one (450 kB = 450000 B, against 450 KiB = 460800 B), so taking it costs the budget nothing and cannot make a passing measurement out of a failing one.
unitConventions.MB: 1000000 bytes (SI), by the same reading and the same reasoning (120 MB = 120000000 B, against 120 MiB = 125829120 B).
unitConventions.MiB: 1048576 bytes (binary). The spec writes `MiB` for the terminal budget explicitly, so this one is not an interpretation.
unitConventions.percentOfOneCore: percent of a single core, averaged over the window the budget's `specTarget` names

measurementProtocol.deterministic: Bundle size, heap at rest, steady heap, and first-ledger-row latency against the fixture's frozen clock gate on any runner.
measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent: Frame time and CPU are measured from the built bundle in the Electron shell against the fixture bridge's flagship scenario with the frozen clock, ten warm-up seconds discarded, the metric taken as the median of three runs, on the pinned CI runner class the desktop workflow names by label, with thresholds calibrated on that class at first landing with 25 % headroom and one automatic re-run before a failure counts.
measurementProtocol.referenceProfile: The `limit` figures are the product targets on the laptop-class reference profile — eight cores, integrated GPU, one 60 Hz display — which the endurance ledger records beside the runner-calibrated thresholds so a runner regression and a product regression stay distinguishable.

budgets.label: Renderer initial bundle
budgets.subject: The gzip-compressed byte total of the CODE the bundler emits on the renderer entry document's initial import graph under `apps/desktop/out/renderer` — the entry module scripts, the `modulepreload` graph, the entry stylesheets, and every chunk reachable from them by a static import — excluding lazy chunks (terminal, node graph, math, diagrams, browser tools), excluding source maps, and excluding the entry HTML document itself. Font files on that same graph are NOT code and are bounded by `renderer-initial-fonts`, in raw bytes; the walk is one walk and every asset on it lands in exactly one of the two rows.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 450 kB gzip, excluding lazy chunks (terminal, node graph, math, diagrams, browser tools)
budgets.notes: Gated on gzip because the product figure is a gzip figure. Brotli is measured and reported for every asset beside it — it is what the renderer protocol handler can actually serve — but it is reported, never gated, so the gate and the spec agree byte for byte. NARROWED to code on 2026-09-08, when `frame/bindings/typeface.ts` first put self-hosted `woff2` faces on the initial graph and took the compressed sum from 446 428 B to 565 084 B. That reading was over the six static cuts of the day; the faces are four variable files now — an upright and an italic per family — and the narrowing is what makes every one of those readings comparable at all. The narrowing is not an exclusion: a `woff2` container is Brotli-compressed already, so gzipping one buys nothing and can cost (the mono face measures 28 B LARGER gzipped than raw), and a sum that folds those in both overstates the total and states it in a unit that describes nothing about how the bytes are served — they are served off the renderer scheme as-is and parsed by no script. The bytes stay bounded, by `renderer-initial-fonts`, in raw bytes. The product figure is unmoved: it and this ceiling are the same 450 kB gzip, over the code that figure was always about.

budgets.label: Renderer initial fonts
budgets.subject: The RAW byte total of every font file on the renderer entry document's initial import graph under `apps/desktop/out/renderer` — the variable `woff2` faces `src/renderer/src/console/frame/bindings/typeface.ts` declares to the document and the bundler emits from that graph, each counted exactly once, with a lazily-loaded chunk's fonts out of scope exactly as its code is.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 232 kB raw over every font on the initial graph
budgets.notes: Minted 2026-09-08 with the narrowing of its sibling `renderer-initial-bundle` to code, so the font bytes are gated rather than excluded. Raw rather than compressed because `woff2` is a Brotli container and gzip over one buys nothing: across the four shipped faces the compressed sum measured 220 441 B against 220 440 B raw on 2026-09-09 — 1 B, 0.0005 %, and pointing the wrong way, since the two mono faces gzip 33 B and 28 B LARGER than they started while the two sans faces come back 6 B and 54 B smaller. Re-derived from `out/renderer/assets` at gzip level 9, which is what `measure-bundle.mts` compresses with, and identical at level 6. A compressed figure here would be an arithmetic fiction stated to more digits of precision than it has. Why 232 kB, why its headroom is 5.2 % rather than the ten percent a smaller subject allowed, and why this is a harness row rather than a product one, are in `harnessBudgetDerivation` — stated once for the set, never copied into a row. Measured on the same walk as its sibling, so the two figures can never disagree about which assets the initial graph holds. The two italic faces are counted here and are requested by a session only when a run matches their rule; a ceiling that bounded only what one session fetched would bound nothing.

budgets.label: Frame time, four lanes streaming
budgets.subject: The 95th-percentile frame duration of the renderer while four agent lanes stream concurrently into the ledger, measured from the built bundle in the Electron shell against the fixture bridge's flagship scenario with the frozen clock. The concurrency is a property of the sampled window rather than a description of it: the harness reads the peak number of runs mid-turn inside its own window off the scenario's beats and fails when it is not one lane per attached agent.
budgets.specTarget: p95 ≤ 16.7 ms on the reference machine
budgets.notes: Hardware-dependent: gates on the pinned CI runner class only, per `measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent`. Off that class the harness still runs and prints the figure — the instrument is exercised everywhere and the comparison is withheld — which `test/console/endurance/pinned-runner-class.ts` decides for the whole tier. The reading is the median of three fresh launches' p95, each sampling 300 frame durations with a warm-up discarded, taken by nearest rank; a frame's duration is measured from the start of its `requestAnimationFrame` callback to the first task that runs after that frame's rendering has been committed, which is the main-thread work the frame cost and not the interval between frames — an interval is bounded below by the surface's own refresh period, so on the 60 Hz reference profile it reads ~16.7 ms for a renderer doing nothing and can never be under this ceiling; the warm-up is a frame count rather than the protocol's ten seconds because a frozen clock walked for ten seconds would deliver the whole script before the first sample, which the harness states in full. No runner-calibrated threshold is recorded yet, so the comparison is against this row's own product limit. The flagship scenario is the four-lane session and its script now drives one: four runs mid-turn at the same tick with interleaved thinking, message, and tool beats, an approval blocking one lane while the other three keep talking, a cost reading per lane, and a helper run threaded to the turn that spawned it. The run asserts three things about its own sampled window rather than describing them — the script finished delivering inside it, it was still arriving during it, and four lanes were streaming inside it, the last read off the scenario's beats by `src/renderer/src/console/bridge/scenario/streaming-lanes.ts` and checked against the scenario's own cast size. Until 2026-09-02 the row was enforced against a skeleton script of eight beats with no assistant or tool row in it at all, so the comparison could stay green over a console that had never streamed anything; that script's own `notMeasurableReason` said as much and was deleted rather than answered. Until 2026-09-02 the harness sampled the interval instead, which is why the row went red on the pinned runner at 16.80 ms while the same tree read 9.90 ms on a 120 Hz laptop: each machine was reporting its own refresh period. Measured after the correction on an eight-core laptop across three passes of the tier: per-run p95 6.80–9.20 ms beside a p50 of 0.10–0.20 ms. Both statistics are printed, because a p50 sitting at the surface's refresh period is the cadence being reported rather than the console's work. The spread is recorded rather than a single figure pinned, because a duration is a property of this machine's CPU as much as of the console — which is the same fact that keeps the comparison on the pinned runner class, and off that class this row gates nothing.

budgets.label: Renderer heap, one session open at rest
budgets.subject: Retained JavaScript heap with one session open and nothing streaming — the console's stores, projections, and persistence layer settled, after a forced garbage collection.
budgets.notes: Deliberately NOT measured in a Node process. Until 2026-09-02 this row was `enforced` against `process.memoryUsage().heapUsed` in the budget CLI with a stand-in entity map retained — no Chromium, no renderer isolate, no React, no DOM, no console store — so the gate could report green over a renderer well past 120 MB, which is the one failure a budget exists to catch. It was then recorded `n/a` rather than re-pointed, because the subject was out of reach: nothing delivered events into a session store, so the only reading available was a renderer with an EMPTY session open. The fixture bridge now serves the growth port's session read and the scenario engine drives beats through the apply chokepoint into it, so the subject exists and the row is gated again — on the endurance tier, which launches the built console, opens the flagship scenario's own session, walks the frozen clock over the whole script, asserts the store admitted events through a live subscription, and reads `performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize` behind a forced collection over a DevTools session, as the minimum over settling samples. The forced collection is what the subject sentence above has always claimed and what the code did not do until 2026-09-05: the precision precondition this tier runs before every gated reading allocates four megabytes and drops them, and a sampler that collects nothing can carry them into the figure the ceiling is compared against. That figure counts allocated-and-not-yet-collected bytes, so it sits at or above the retained heap this row bounds, which is the safe direction for a ceiling. The reading is a renderer isolate figure taken in the Electron shell in unobtrusive-window mode; the substrate floor recorded on 2026-09-02 with no session content was 6,564,912 B.

budgets.label: Steady heap, flagship live stream
budgets.subject: Renderer heap over thirty minutes of the flagship scenario streaming live on the scenario clock — both its ceiling and its slope, since a heap that stays under the ceiling while climbing monotonically is still a leak.
budgets.specTarget: flat over thirty minutes; ≤ 250 MB renderer heap
additionalCriteria: The heap is flat over the thirty-minute stream: no monotonic growth across the run's snapshot series.
budgets.notMeasurableReason: The endurance tier and its heap instrument now exist — `test/console/endurance/heap-instrument.ts` forces a collection over a CDP `HeapProfiler` session, `steady-state.test.ts` bounds heap GROWTH across 200 churn cycles that stream the in-tree flagship script through the fixture bridge once, and `heap-at-rest.test.ts` gates the at-rest ceiling — and none of the three conditions THIS row states is met by that. No run holds the console for thirty minutes: the `console-endurance-body` allowance is nine. No snapshot SERIES is analysed for slope: `memlab` is a manifest dependency now and `heap-snapshot-analysis.ts` reads a single snapshot by constructor, which answers what one heap is holding rather than whether a run's heap climbed, so the flat-over-thirty-minutes criterion still has no verdict behind it. And there is no dated endurance ledger to record a refutation in.
budgets.notes: This reading belongs on the endurance tier — heap snapshots captured by an own CDP helper, analyzed with memlab, results in a dated ledger.

budgets.label: Idle CPU, session open, nothing streaming
budgets.subject: CPU consumed by the renderer with a session open and no stream running, averaged over sixty seconds — together with the assertion that no timer fires in that window except the refresh scheduler's deadline and the presence heartbeat.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 0.5 % of one core averaged over sixty seconds; no timer fires except the refresh scheduler's deadline and the presence heartbeat
additionalCriteria: No timer fires during the sixty-second window except the refresh scheduler's absolute deadline and the presence heartbeat.
budgets.notMeasurableReason: No harness on any tier samples renderer CPU, so the sixty-second average is not taken. The criterion beside it is not taken either: it names what FIRED inside that window, and no tier watches a running renderer's timers — `no-restricted-globals` in `eslint.config.mjs` refuses `setInterval` in renderer source, which is the different claim this row's notes already distinguish. The subject is in tree — the endurance tier opens the flagship session route in the built shell and `console/store/read/refresh-scheduler.ts` owns every refresh — so what is missing is the instrument, which the endurance reference run still owes.
budgets.notes: Hardware-dependent: gates on the pinned CI runner class only, per `measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent`. The timer-enumeration half is a lint rule (`no-restricted-globals` on `setInterval`, in `eslint.config.mjs`), not a number.

budgets.label: Streaming CPU, one lane
budgets.subject: CPU consumed by the renderer while one agent lane streams into the ledger, together with the assertion that the reveal engine yields when the frame budget is spent rather than overrunning it.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 15 % of one core on the reference machine; the reveal engine yields when the frame budget is spent
additionalCriteria: The reveal engine yields when the frame budget is spent.
budgets.notMeasurableReason: No harness on any tier samples renderer CPU. The subject is in tree — `console/bridge/scenario/streaming-lanes.ts` drives four lanes and `frame-time.test.ts` measures a window it asserts they were streaming inside — so what is missing is the instrument, which the endurance reference run still owes.
budgets.notes: Hardware-dependent: gates on the pinned CI runner class only, per `measurementProtocol.hardwareDependent`.

budgets.label: Terminal instance
budgets.subject: Retained memory of one `terminal` pane instance at the default scrollback — the `@xterm/xterm` instance, its WebGL renderer, and the pane's own state.
budgets.notes: The row was `enforced` for one day, 2026-09-02, against a harness that constructed `XtermTerminalAdapter` directly under happy-dom and sampled the Node process's own heap — a subject narrower than this row's own sentence, which can report green over a pane well past the ceiling — and it was then recorded `n/a` rather than re-pointed, because no deck mounted panes and there was nothing whole to hold. It is gated again from the endurance tier, which now has one: `console/frame/pane-harness/PaneHarnessSurface.tsx` is a `define`-gated fixture surface, reached at `#/pane-harness/<paneKind>/<sessionId>`, that resolves the body through the deck's own `ConsolePaneRegistry` and mounts one more instance per press. So the subject is held WHOLE — the built console in a real Electron window, a `terminal` pane the registry resolved, mounted through a real React commit, its emulator on a live WebGL2 context, bound to a session the scenario engine has delivered into — and each of those is asserted rather than assumed: the run FAILS on a `dom` renderer reading rather than measuring the fallback, and fails on an empty session store rather than folding a lease off an empty log. WHAT THE HARNESS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT HOLD is the deck: no tab strip, no layout, no drag target, no detach path. That is closer to this row's sentence than a deck-mounted reading would be — the ceiling is per INSTANCE, and a figure taken inside a deck would fold the deck's own cost into it and report a pane over budget for chrome the row does not name. The figure is the difference between the settled renderer heap with no instance open and with one, taken as the minimum over settling samples, after a warm-up cycle that moves the emulator chunk's one-time cost to the left of the baseline; two further instances are then opened and their per-instance slope is required to agree with that figure, which is the control against a fixed cost being reported as the instance. The adapter-level claims that ARE reachable in a Node process — scrollback eviction, disposal, and a working day of pane churn — stay on `terminal-endurance.test.ts` beside the churn accounting they belong with; that file makes NO ceiling claim of its own, so neither half of the instance ever receives an independent allowance. WHAT THE FIGURE COVERS: the instance is priced as ONE populated pane — the mounted pane's standing cost plus a full buffer at the default scrollback, both measured at one width (`TERMINAL_BUDGET_MEASUREMENT_COLUMNS`) and one depth (`TERMINAL_DEFAULT_SCROLLBACK_LINES`, both in the cap home) and summed before a single `evaluateBudget` call. Measured 2026-09-04 on macOS: 16,456 kB of 20,480 kB (80.4 %) — pane 940 kB plus scrollback 15,516 kB at 10,000 lines × 120 columns; later panes 823 kB each; 417 kB still held after three closed; a second run reproduced the sum within 10 kB. That headroom is thin on purpose: the next thing that grows a terminal pane moves this figure, and changing either cap-home constant changes what the row means. WHAT IT CANNOT YET: the scrollback half is still driven in the driver process, because the byte stream, the scrollback, and the resize report are a growth-slate row and no wire in this revision can put a line into a MOUNTED pane — so the sum is conservative (it omits nothing the mounted pane holds and adds the buffer the pane would hold), and the day that row lands the harness drives bytes into the mounted pane and the two halves collapse into one delta. The readings are taken behind a forced collection over a DevTools session rather than from the sampler alone: a difference of a few hundred kilobytes is decided by WHEN the collector ran, and without it this same code measured a first instance at 4,165 kB and a per-instance slope of minus 5,765 kB.

budgets.label: Time to first ledger row on launch
budgets.subject: Elapsed time from window show to the first ledger row painted, in fixture mode against the frozen clock.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 800 ms from window show, fixture mode
budgets.notes: Deterministic against the fixture's frozen clock, so it gates on any runner once the ledger exists — it is not one of the two hardware-dependent budgets. Window show is read as the renderer's own `first-contentful-paint` entry: `revealWindow` is called from `ready-to-show`, which Electron emits once the page has been rendered, and on macOS an automated launch deliberately never reveals the window at all — so there is no `show` timestamp to read and no wall clock is read in either process. The interval ends at the animation frame after the first row element is laid out, and the whole of it is measured inside one page function, so the only harness cost inside it is the gap between the launch handshake settling and that function starting, which the report prints separately rather than subtracting. Measured 43–46 ms of an 800 ms ceiling on an eight-core laptop across three runs of the tier, 13–22 ms of it that handshake.

budgets.label: Console launch readiness ladder
budgets.subject: Wall time from `_electron.launch()` to the renderer's frame element being present — the whole cold-start ladder (first window, `load`, the frame selector) charged once between its phases rather than once each.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 30 000 ms across every readiness phase combined
budgets.notes: The whole cold-start ladder — first window, `load`, the frame selector — charged once between its phases rather than once each, which is what the four independent 30 000 ms allowances this replaced got wrong. Generous on purpose: a cold CI runner with no warm Electron cache is the case it must not flake on. The derivation these three bounds share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Measured by `test/helpers/launch-deadline.test.ts`, which drives the real `LaunchDeadline` this ladder draws from and holds the aggregate against every launching tier's resolved patience.

budgets.label: Console launch first-frame witness
budgets.subject: The wait, after the renderer reports ready, for the first animation frame to arrive — the reading that separates a window that painted from one that merely opened.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 15 000 ms from readiness, not from launch
budgets.notes: Armed only once readiness has landed, so a slow boot is charged to the readiness row rather than reported as a frame that never came — the flake this split was introduced to remove. What it answers is whether the window painted at all, and late is not the same as never: it fails only on never. First-frame LATENCY is bounded by nothing here — `frame-time-p95-four-lanes` is `enforced` and does catch a frame-schedule regression, but its subject is the p95 of a streaming window rather than the first paint, and it compares only on the pinned runner class — so a green witness is a claim about paint and never about how long the paint took. The derivation these three bounds share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Measured by the suite that drives the race rather than by the one that reads the figure: `test/helpers/frame-witness.test.ts` constructs the real `FrameWitness` over a source that delivers late and one that never delivers, which is the boundary this bound decides. It named `test/helpers/launch-deadline.test.ts` until 2026-09-05, a file that holds this figure against its constant and drives no witness at all.

budgets.label: Console launch cleanup
budgets.subject: The bound `application.close()` is raced against before the Electron process tree is SIGKILLed and the temporary profile removed.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 10 000 ms, or the tree is terminated
budgets.notes: A ceiling rather than a target: what it guards against is an Electron wedged rather than slow, so what matters is that some finite number is enforced. It is the WHOLE applied bound and the same one on both closing paths — a close reached from a failed launch is held to it exactly as one reached minutes later on the success path is, so the figure a budget audit reads is the figure the harness enforces. It was a floor until 2026-09-04, raised by whatever the launch deadline had left, which handed an early readiness failure nearly the whole 55 000 ms deadline. Because `terminated` records and passes, this figure decides when the process tree is SIGKILLed rather than whether the tier goes red; `unterminable` and `closed-after-rejection` fail, and those are the two settlements that harm the launches after them. The derivation these three bounds share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`. Measured by `test/helpers/bounded-cleanup.test.ts`, which races a real `BoundedCleanup` against a close that never settles and one that rejects; it named `test/helpers/launch-deadline.test.ts` until 2026-09-05, which applies this bound to nothing.

budgets.label: Console launch test-body allowance
budgets.subject: The wall time a test body gets between a settled launch and its cleanup — the interval `withLaunchedConsole` runs the caller's own function in, and the default for a tier that states no allowance of its own.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 70 000 ms between a settled launch and its cleanup
budgets.notes: Counted from the worst body in the tree rather than chosen, and RE-COUNTED on 2026-09-05 once every wait in that body was made to draw on this allowance. `e2e/colour-scheme-lost-on-reload.test.ts` declares, in order: the palette overlay opening at 10 000 ms; three 10 000 ms `expect.poll` waits, on the applied attribute, on the durable write, and on the attribute after a reload — 30 000 ms in all; and the reload, whose navigation and the frame element it must produce share ONE 30 000 ms clock, because the renderer boot they perform between them is the same subject `console-launch-readiness` bounds. 10 000 + 30 000 + 30 000 is this figure. The 60 000 it replaces counted the polls and the reload and omitted the overlay wait, which carried Playwright's default rather than any figure written down here. A bound under a body's own declared waits would fire first and replace that body's message ("the scheme did not change") with a sentence about a clock, which is the inversion the launch deadline exists to undo. A body is handed what is LEFT of this allowance and asks for `boundedMs(<its own bound>)`, the smaller of the two, so the first wait that cannot fit fails with ITS sentence rather than the generic overrun. That every bounded wait in a launching tier draws on the allowance is a reviewer's check — `apps/desktop/AGENTS.md` states it — rather than a source scan. The derivation these rows share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`.

budgets.label: Console endurance test-body allowance
budgets.subject: The wall time the endurance tier's sustained workload gets between a settled launch and its cleanup — hundreds of driven churn cycles and the settling heap samples either side of them.
budgets.specTarget: ≤ 540 000 ms between a settled launch and its cleanup
budgets.notes: A separate figure because the endurance body is a different subject from an end-to-end one, not a slower version of it: `steady-state.test.ts` drives 200 churn cycles twice over with settling heap samples either side, which its own count comment measures at roughly 50 ms a cycle — well under a minute warm, and the reason that tier has always carried a patience an order of magnitude past the end-to-end one. Nine minutes puts the derived tier timeout at 607 000 ms, which is `tierTimeoutFor(540 000)` read off its own constants: `LAUNCH_BUDGET_MS` of 65 000 — 30 000 readiness plus 15 000 frame witness plus `CLEANUP_PHASES` × 10 000 cleanup — then this allowance, then the 2 000 ms settlement residual. It read 597 000 here while the cleanup slice was one phase rather than two, so the figure moved when `CLEANUP_PHASES` became 2 and this note did not; nothing about a tier nobody has complained about is tightened by either. Its own waits draw on this allowance through the same `boundedMs` the end-to-end bodies use, but this FIGURE is deliberately not re-counted from them: a churn cycle's declared bounds are ceilings for a wedged console rather than intervals a run spends, and 200 of them summed would describe no run this tier has ever performed. The derivation these rows share is stated once in `harnessBudgetDerivation`.
